items.body: Run by our very own Joseph Sannicandro, the Lost Children Net Label has been quiet as a Bandcamp imprint, but kept alive through Joseph’s podcasts and newsletter posts since the 2022 release of the massive 56-track [Useless Sounds]. Returning in full force with a triptych of tapes, Lost Children is ready to reclaim its place at the forefront of experimental music. The crown jewel of the bundle is CRACKS, a gathering of international musicians who address the “concept of the border as a colonial wound.” Proceeds benefit the Council on American-Islamic Relations Minnesota and Lumpen Radio (an initiative of the Public Media Institute in Chicago). The confrontational words on the cover have become a global rallying cry. Joni Void starts the set off with “Borders,” cutting right to the chase. The percussion sounds like a jailer’s baton dragged across prison bars. A connection is made between physical borders, sonic borders and the borders of perception, with dialogue interrupted by the siren and blare of a local enforcement agent. Martín Rodríguez shares radio transmissions heard from the Arizona-Mexico border where he was raised, giving credit to radio for helping him to recover from a brain tumor. The transmissions sparkle and fade, as if underlining the name of the Lost Children imprint. One thinks of voices and souls lost and the search for missing loved ones, possibly deported, possibly dead. Kate Carr offers bucolic bells bisected by the essential chaos of street protests, suggesting that the comfortable must be disturbed in order for substantive change to unfold. Lubo Alexandrov‘s bucolic “Echoes (from the other side)” doesn’t identify which side it refers to, leaving the interpretation wide open. Speaker Music‘s haunting, echoed, abraded and ultimately percussive “Moral Injury” exposes the deepest rupture of the crisis as an affront to goodness itself. Sannicandro’s own “rethink not reform” brings the sound to the streets, the appealing “Wait” of an electronic crossing signal contrasted with a sense that the fragile peace is about to be disturbed; in layers of increasing ferocity, it is. The disorientation of the intimate soundscape imitates that of the assaulted. apartment52‘s “i would die for anything, maybe” exposes a different insecurity while repeating the effect of messages that fail to get through. A heartfelt live recording from Hamza Lahmadi connects the yearning of sojourners around the world, who just want a place to call home. Mai Mai Mai incorporates waves as siren call, implying both the hope of welcome and the lack of permission to land. The drone is lonely and isolated, the land right there. Anas Hajam lightens the mood a bit with finger-picking goodness and breath; one needs encouragement such as this. Then Joni Void returns as the remixer of Soledad Rosas‘ “Piel,” which extends the references to breath along with vocal glissandos and tender song. The intake just prior to the second minute recalls George Floyd. Only a minute long, Esther B.‘s “molti sport” is a rush of static awaiting definition. Then comes a reference to Greek mythology: thenewobjective feat. Cole Pulice use “Scylla and Charybdis” to reference the idiom “the lesser of two evils,” summarizing the current state of border disputes, in which no one wins. Stefan Christoff closes the compilation with “Turn,” whose tolling church bells, echoed on prepared piano, are both indictment and call to arms. Two artists featured on CRACKS also branch out across the bundle. ATMOSPHERICS is taken from a series of soundscape broadcasts prepared by Diana Duta & Stefan Christoff. Partially recorded on the silver anniversary of Portugal’s Carnation Revolution, “Paysage sonare” is a tribute to victory, a long battle finally won. The sounds of the coast are sounds of peace in both senses of the word. Soft ambient tones unify the composition, wresting control from the field recordings in the tenth minute before ceding space in the eighteenth and again in the thirty-first, ending in familial laughter and joy. Similar sounds launch the title track, recorded in Brussels. The piece eventually branches into the northern marshes, calling on hydrophones for a glance below the surface. The contrast between city and marsh recalls CRACKS: the discussion of desirable environments, “migration, political dissent and resistance.” The link becomes overt in the chants of the twenty-first minute. Again Christoff’s synth, along with pensive guitar, is the glue that holds the work together, although even this is lost in time, rescued from older tapes, a subtle metaphor. In the long aquatic segment that closes the piece, one feels retreat and resolution. Esther B. is also Esther Bourdages, whose cassette Listening session, live concerts, figure skating “turns the turntable into a destructive instrument.” These live improvisations expose the turntable as preserver and destroyer of memory. Segments rise through the ether intact, only to be savaged with love. There’s a huge difference between turntablism in a hip-hop sense and turntablism in an experimental sense, but the two are not exclusive. In her preference for the older, even archival records, Bourdages honors The Caretaker; in her disdain for the creation of linear narratives or danceable samples, she honors Kid Koala. “figure skating” flips the script, conflating the stylus and the skate, the vinyl and the ice, with few if any identifiable markers until the end: a mesmerizing lesson in abstraction and a companion to Curling. In “Earache, My Eye,” a horrified son protests to his father, “You ruined my record, man!” Such a thing does not exist in Bourdages’ world, where records are purposely altered by “grinding, cutting and sanding.” If anything, the imperfections are the draw. Yet it is obvious that the artist loves her collection, teasing sounds from these records that were never intended to be heard, like coaxing stories from a childhood friend. It is passing strange to hear them on a cassette, although in the hands of another this might be manipulated in a different way, then passed to a digital specialist for further dismantling. We once thought that sound, once recorded, was fixed; we believe so no longer. Welcome back, Lost Children! (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by WaldoJeffers — As someone who really enjoys Conrad Schnitzler's early work with Kluster, Tangerine Dream and also solo, I consider "Gold" to be a highly convincing album, standing in the tradition of "Blau" and certainly "Rot", dating from the same creative period as this belatedly released album.Schnitzler experiments here once again with all sorts of electronically generated instruments; briefly, I even hear an accordion. You will search in vain for rhythms and harmonies here, of course; "Gold" is an album of free form. It chirps, pings and creaks merrily away; only in track 12 (the tracks have no titles) does something almost akin to a dance mood arise as a result of the electronic percussion; although even to this you can hardly dance, there is simply too much going on. An oriental-sounding flute improvises over heavy chirping and bubbling above the quasi-soloing percussion. Space techno? With the following track, "13", which sounds like a cool, empty factory hall turned into music, a bit of Industrial also comes into play."Gold" is fun and enormously entertaining for those people who (like me) find many of the productions of the "Berlin School" incredibly boring. Not a typical Conrad Schnitzler album, but for me (perhaps for that very reason) one of the best.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — ProjeKct Three's 'Masque' comes straight from the R&D department of King Crimson. This is the thirdinstallment in the live project series featuring members of the 'THRAK' lineup of the Robert Fripp-led band, brought together with the aim of exploring off-beat ideas through improvisation andexperimentation. These are live recordings featuring alternating lineups of the 90s Crimson, withthis particular 1999 recording featuring the trio of Robert Fripp, Trey Gunn, and Pat Mastelotto. Asis the case with the majority of the KC releases from that period, the music played by ProjeKctThree incorporates the spacey ambient soundscapes patented by Fripp, together with the finely tunedWarr guitar of Trey Gunn and the impressive array of electronic percussion and loops played by PatMastelotto. The type of experimental rock presented on 'Masque', however, is more abstract and lessgroovy than the output of other ProjeKcts (like One or Two, which makes it closer to something like'Thrakattak' than the album 'THRAK' itself.The thirteen tracks making up this live album are numbered and (perhaps suggestively) left untitled,while the somewhat intimidating, surreal and impersonal cover art uncannily reflects the kind ofmusic played on 'Masque'. This is one of these experimental recordings that only make sense whenheard in their entirety, but if I were to outline several pieces of greater significance, I wouldhave to start with '1', which is an obnoxious and impulsive opener, replete with hefty bass tonesand obscure guitar licks. 'Masque 2' then presents a more sustained rock sound tinted with gentleambient soundscapes, while the complex rhythms on '3' weave around the haunting electronics in arather menacing way. Later on, 'Masque 7' represents another abstract-sided piece, impressing with asoft but prominent bass sound, whereas the industrial hue encompassing 'Masque 8' makes it one ofthe darker compositions heard on this album. It is also worth noting how effective the hypnoticallyabrasive sounds on '9' are, with the two final pieces also being among the highlights.Of all the ProjeKcts, Three might be the single most intriguing variation of Crimson - 'Masque' isunorthodox and compelling, but for me this is the kind of experimentation that drives the genreforward.

items.body: Review by AWizardATrueAimee — I've got quite the history with this album since my husband, who introduced me to progressive rock, had an email referring to it. That was back in 2009 and I've listened to it countless times since. I was so excited to see the band was releasing a remaster and I certainly have not been disappointed by it. Steve Wilson did such a great job on their other releases. I'll admit I was heartbroken but understanding that this album could present some difficulties. There's been some concerns about AI being used in this remaster that I somewhat understand but?. I don't think we'll be getting as clear and true of a version of this album otherwise. And if this is the way it's got to be done, I'm here for the ride. This remaster/remix showed me all sorts of instruments and sections that I didn't hear in the past which I'm really grateful for. An album which at times was previously impossible to parse is now much punchy and emotionally charged than ever. And the album title track has always rang to me as a Gentle Giant staple within their catalogue. It doesn't get much more progressive than this.

items.body: Impressed by this partnership’s Dvořák Ninth (review), I was eager to hear their Bruckner fourth, surely the composer’s most popular symphony both in the concert hall and on record. This new reading, while impressive, is not a complete success. Symphony No. 4 Amazon Presto Apple This reading lacks the instrumental weight and depth of color that I would argue makes for an authentic Bruckner sound. Having grown up listening to many Telarc recordings of this orchestra, I lay the blame for this deficiency on the engineering. The mics are placed too close to the musicians, surely to minimize audience noise during this live recording. There is little bloom to the sound, and no real hall ambience. Climaxes feel contained, and softer dynamics are limited by the proximity of the mics. Bruckner’s music was written with a warm, reverberant acoustic in mind, and that acoustic is an integral part of the sound. Not so here. Instead, it is like standing one foot away from Seurat’s A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte: every brush stroke is visible, and we might appreciate how the painting is assembled, but it comes at the cost of the image’s beauty, mystery and expression. The second issue has to do with the edition. There are now ten different editions of the fourth symphony to choose from. Stutzmann uses the late Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs’ 2021 critical edition of the 1878–81 version, which has been recorded only once before, by Simon Rattle with the LSO (LSO Live). For that album Cohrs described his edition as “the second version of the ‘Romantic’ Symphony as it stood by the end of 1881,” including “Bruckner’s own suggested cut in the Finale.” But Stutzmann does not take the cut — why not? Why embrace a little-known version and then ignore one of its most significant, composer-sanctioned changes? The liner notes offer no discussion of the edition, nor is it listed on either side of the booklet cover. As to the performance itself, I had initially intended to limit comparisons to other American recordings, but it now seems best to set Stutzmann against Rattle (details – review). His performance is faster, with an overall timing of 61’30” against Stutzmann’s 71’39”, and the largest difference comes in the final movement, where Stutzmann restores the passage Bruckner marked for cutting. Each conductor belongs to a different interpretive school. Rattle recalls Karajan: a subtle use of rubato, polished orchestral sound with resplendent brass and gossamer strings, a unified pulse that keeps the structure in view. Stutzmann is far closer to Jochum: much freer rubato, a more heterogeneous orchestral sound and, more distinctively, an intensely songful rendering of Bruckner’s score. Nathalie Stutzmann conducts the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra. Photo © Rand Lines. Stutzmann’s approach is compelling in the second movement, though at 17’05” it feels more Adagio than Bruckner’s Andante quasi Allegretto. In the finale the flexibility sometimes compromises a sense of the overarching structure, and there are moments when the energy level dips precipitously low. This is less of an issue in the opening movement, where one does get to hear much of the contrapuntal inner voices. Both Rattle and Stutzmann solicit rounded articulation, and I often missed the cut and thrust of Blomstedt’s San Francisco account on Decca and Honeck’s Pittsburgh performance on Reference, especially in the Scherzo. Both drive the music harder, encouraging more wildness in the trumpet-capped climaxes. Bruckner described the Trio as “how a barrel-organ plays during the midday meal in the forest.” Honeck is perhaps best at capturing this rustic picture, even if he is reticent to allow an earthier, less refined sound. Stutzmann conjures a poised, lightly sprung elegance that I enjoyed, even though it hardly captures the composer’s description. In short, I find Stutzmann’s performance the more compelling of the two. Yet if I want to hear this edition, surely I want Bruckner’s cut in the finale. Rattle’s release adds to the symphony itself the discarded 1874/76 Scherzo and the 1878 Volksfest Finale, an extended early version of the Andante, and the unabridged 1881 Finale, a valuable addition for Bruckner specialists. Ultimately, neither recording compels me to embrace this version over the more familiar Haas and Nowak editions, and neither matches the brilliance of Blomstedt, Honeck, or the classic Böhm/Vienna/Decca. items.body: Mitsuko Uchida’s 2025 live performance of the late Beethoven sonatas (Op. 109–111) arrives almost two decades after her studio recording for Decca, and it carries the added weight of being her final account of these works. Her choice of Suntory Hall marks a homecoming: she has played there since the hall’s opening season in 1986, and remains its only Associate Artist. Last Three Sonatas Amazon Presto Apple The gap between the two readings naturally raises the question of how much her interpretations have developed. If we go by Op. 109, things have indeed changed: not a drastic pivot, but an amplification of certain aspects. The 2006 reading already had an appreciable fluidity, but in the newer Vivace (track 1) Uchida makes more unabashed pauses and rubatos that still fit naturally into the music. Some of the urgency of the earlier second movement has turned into greater dramatic power here, and the attention to articulation and secondary voices is never sacrificed. The temperament of the final movement (track 3) can vary considerably depending on the tempo of the opening theme. Where Serkin and Gilels move more slowly and evoke contemplation, Uchida is brisker than either of them, and her pace captures the cantabile of Beethoven’s marking. In the variations that follow, a deep familiarity reveals itself in her ability to balance forward motion against the emphasis the grandest moments need. Op. 110 comes alive through contrast. Uchida uses Beethoven’s textures to shift between lyricism and resonance. The arpeggios at the start of the Moderato cantabile (track 4), leading up to the second theme, are a prime example: they begin as shimmering filigree and morph into a resplendent presence — perhaps a fitting representation of the vocal and orchestral sides she brings out throughout. The Scherzo carries a much higher degree of austerity and insistence than the 2006 Decca version, though both readings remain entirely valid. The Adagio (track 6) reveals a performer who understands the profundity of late Beethoven: the desperation, the melancholy with its sharp poignancy, the gravitas of internal conflict and weariness. What is most captivating is her ability to convey the rawness of these sentiments in a live setting. Uchida’s Fuga (track 7) proves more multidimensional than many. The switch from minor to major is subtle, and it gives her room to explore the quieter sides of the fugue before it spins into something much larger. Even in the softest playing nothing sounds hurried. Pauses are placed to maximize dynamic contrast while delineating the intricacies of Beethoven’s structure. Mitsuko Uchida. Photo © Justin Pumfrey / Decca. Although it moves slightly slower at times than her previous interpretation, the new Op. 111 (tracks 8–9) embodies the severity and boldness of the Maestoso marking. The urgency of the prior account has developed into an equally compelling adamance. The calmness of the Arietta feels like an arrival after a long journey. The same weighty substance carries into the variations, which works for the most part, though the syncopated variation at 6’40” could take a touch more rhythmic vitality. What emerges most strongly, though, is the intricacy of the tender moments, which linger in their transcendence. The engineers have kept audience noise to a minimum, and the piano is captured with enough clarity to register its tone and regulation. As a final account of these sonatas this is a distinguished one, and the culmination of Uchida’s long engagement with them. items.body: Saint-Saëns completed his Symphony No. 3 in 1886, commissioned by the Philharmonic Society of London, and conducted the premiere himself at the age of fifty. It was the last symphony he would write, and it came at the height of his career. He is said to have remarked that he would never achieve anything like it again. When Franz Liszt died later that year, Saint-Saëns dedicated the score to his memory. The “Organ” nickname is a little misleading. The composer wrote not a concerto but a symphony “with organ,” where the instrument works inside the orchestra rather than in front of it. The scoring also calls for a piano, played at times by two players. The four traditional movements are folded into two continuous parts, unified by a single theme that keeps returning in new forms, a technique absorbed from Liszt. The music travels from restless C minor to a blazing C major finale, whose massive organ entrance has tested engineers as much as conductors. Recordings have answered that challenge in different ways, from concert-hall organs captured in place to a cathedral instrument recorded separately and mixed in. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Saint-Saëns’s Symphony No. 3 (“Organ”). Boston Symphony Orchestra, Charles Munch More than sixty years after it was made, Charles Munch’s 1959 recording in Boston remains the one to beat. The thrill comes from playing of scorching intensity that unfolds like a live concert. Munch sets a fast tempo for the first movement’s main theme, and the rhythmic drive never lets up. The strings sing the *Poco adagio* with unforced lyricism, a reminder that this performance is not all fire. In the finale, Berj Zamkochian’s organ makes a thunderous entrance, its bass seeming to shake the floor. The aging tape strains audibly under that huge chord, yet the drama sweeps this flaw aside. Add Munch’s Debussy *La Mer* and Ibert *Escales* as couplings, and the disc’s legendary status is easy to understand. Munch Amazon Presto Apple Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Daniel Barenboim The organ heard on Daniel Barenboim’s 1976 Chicago recording was played an ocean away from the orchestra. Gaston Litaize recorded his part on the organ of Chartres Cathedral, and the two performances were joined afterward in the studio. That procedure could easily have sounded artificial, but the combined result has an epic, almost otherworldly presence. It crowns a performance of irresistible panache, with the Chicago brass playing at full strength and a finale of colossal impact. Barenboim’s invigorating first-movement tempo leaves the strings a little untidy in places, a small price for the sweep he achieves. It matches Munch for voltage while sounding far more modern. For the symphony’s raw physical thrill, this is the version to reach for. Barenboim Amazon Presto Apple Detroit Symphony Orchestra, Paul Paray Paul Paray’s 1957 Detroit account moves with exceptional lightness. Its appeal is not weight or blaze, but transparency and grace. Paray trained this orchestra himself, and it shows in the supple phrasing and the way every strand stays audible. Tempos are bracingly fast, yet nothing feels rushed. The playing stays composed even at full speed. The organ part is in the hands of Marcel Dupré, one of the great virtuosos of the twentieth century. Made with just three microphones, the recording remains astonishingly fresh for its age, clearer than Munch’s. For listeners who want to hear the elegance inside this symphony, Paray is the essential alternative. Paray Amazon Presto Apple Montreal Symphony Orchestra, Charles Dutoit Few discs did more to show off the young CD format than Charles Dutoit’s 1982 Montreal recording. Its lasting virtues, though, are musical: elastic, beautifully controlled phrasing and orchestral playing of rare polish. Peter Hurford’s organ is cleanly focused and never distorts, even in the loudest pages. Every detail sits in natural proportion. The coupling is the Second Piano Concerto, with Pascal Rogé as soloist. Those who crave the sheer force of Munch or Barenboim may find Dutoit reserved. Anyone meeting the symphony for the first time could not ask for a better guide. Dutoit Amazon Presto Apple Kansas City Symphony, Michael Stern Glorious sound is the first thing anyone notices about Michael Stern’s 2013 recording with the Kansas City Symphony. It is not, however, the main reason to recommend the album. The performance underneath has genuine vitality, with crisp rhythms and the rich, full-bodied sonority this music thrives on. Jan Kraybill presides over a big Casavant concert organ, and the recording gives it impressive depth and space. The couplings are generous: the *Introduction and Rondo capriccioso* with violinist Noah Geller, and the lesser-known *La Muse et le Poète*. A performance this alive earns its place beside the classics. Stern Amazon Presto Apple Top image ©️ The Classic Review, AI generated The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: The members of the Norwegian trio Tazer introduce themselves only by their aliases: ‘CALICO’, ‘ONI-X01’, and ‘DRUMNIBAL’. Beyond that, they prefer to keep an air of mystery – something I won’t attempt to unravel here. Their focus is on the music rather than the people behind it, and rightly so. I first discovered Tazer through their earlier EP, but it is their self-released debut album, “Taze Is The Rule”, that truly demands attention. It has been a long time since a debut record has hit me with this kind of force. This is pure sonic aggression, forged from a relentless fusion of EBM, Metal, and Techno. Every track is crushingly heavy, leaving nothing standing in its wake. The songs strike with the intensity of an imaginary war machine, determined to conquer dark dance floors and every poor soul brave enough to step onto them. Tazer sounds like an explosion whose full impact has yet to be measured. Fortunately, the band took the time to answer a few questions and shed some light on the ideas, influences, and vision behind “Taze Is The Rule”. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Tazer ‘Taze Is The Rule’ interview Q: Let’s start by clearing up a few things: where do Tazer and the project’s name come from? Who is behind the aliases, and what has your musical journey been like up to this point? CALICO: The Tazer project officially kicked off in 2024 when we wrote our first EP, “9001 Volts”. We chose the name Tazer because we wanted something that felt high-voltage but was also instantly recognizable. A small taser can pack a massive punch, and that just felt like the perfect metaphor for our energy. As for our aliases, they are symbols. Honestly, who we are behind them really doesn’t matter, we are our music, and we prefer to let the tracks do the talking. Q: What have been the key influences and sources of inspiration behind your music, and what does this particular form of expression mean to you? ONI-X01: We’ve always been massive fans of bands like Rammstein and Combichrist, but we really wanted to inject our own flavor into the mix. The goal was to create something heavy and raw, but also immediate and danceable. By mixing Metal with classic EBM elements, we want to hit people right in the gut and pull them into a completely new kind of mindset. Q: How did this debut album come together, and how were the songwriting and production responsibilities divided among the band members? Looking back, what were the biggest challenges you faced while creating it? DRUMNIBAL: This album is the result of years of hard work. Out of the 10 tracks we originally wrote, 5 of them ended up on the “9001 Volts” EP. So, over the next two years, we had to write 5 brand-new tracks to bring the album back to 10. During that time, our sound naturally evolved and the line-up shifted into the trio we are today. Our creative process is pretty organic: we usually start with electronic riffs, build a solid structure, and then layer on the guitars, bass, and vocals. Lyrics always come last because they depend entirely on the vibe and emotion the music triggers in us. We write everything together as a team, no strict division of labor, just pure collaboration. Q: If I understand correctly, “Taze Is The Rule” is more than just an album title – it also serves as a kind of manifesto for the band. Both lyrically and musically, the track comes across as hard-hitting, provocative, and uncompromising. Could you elaborate on that? What does it reveal about your perspective on the world and the society we live in? ONI-X01: You hit the nail on the head. “Taze Is The Rule” is our manifesto, our creed, and our undeniable truth. It all started with this first track, which really opened our eyes and made us realize exactly what we wanted to create. We feel like the world is lacking a bit of discipline right now; everything seems to get lost in superficial noise and trivial complaints that don’t really lead anywhere. That’s why we felt the need to forge music that brings back some of that discipline, giving people an ideal to rally behind with a sound that’s tough, but fair. Q: Both your music and visual identity seem perfectly suited for the live stage. What have your experiences been like so far, and what can audiences expect from a Tazer performance? DRUMNIBAL: Throughout our musical journeys, we’ve spent enough time on stage to consider ourselves live veterans. However, with this specific project, we are completely rethinking our approach to live shows to deliver something genuinely fresh and powerful. We know it’s a challenge, ‘cause the live scene is incredibly competitive right now, and coming up with original ideas takes a lot of the discipline we talk about. We apply that same focus to our music videos, carefully crafting our identity through every choice of makeup, wardrobe, storyline, and camera angle. Q: Are you already working on new material or perhaps even a follow-up album? Do you have a clear vision of how Tazer will evolve in the future and where you would like to take the project? CALICO: We definitely have a long-term plan, which includes diving into a second album. We already have some ideas cooking that we hope people will love. Right now, though, the main focus of that plan is locking down and developing our live shows. We honestly can’t wait to bring these tracks to the stage and connect with the crowd under the banner of ‘Taze is the Rule’. About Tazer Tazer is a Norwegian electro-industrial project formed in 2024 by musicians performing under the aliases CALICO, ONI-X01, and DRUMNIBAL, and signed to Hellektrokution Records. The band debuted with the single “A Razor Can Slit, A Tazer Can Kill” on 5 November 2024, followed by the self-released EP “9001 Volts” on 21 December 2024. Of the ten tracks the band had written by then, five appeared on that EP; the remaining five, plus five newly written tracks, became the ten-track debut album “Taze Is The Rule”, released via Hellektrokution Records on 30 April 2026. The album combines EBM, industrial metal and techno, with influences including Rammstein and Combichrist. Tazer returned in October 2025 with a Halloween video for “I Put a Spell on You”, and in May 2026 released the single “Raise The Voltage”, the album’s fifth track, via Hellektrokution Records, Spotify, YouTube and Bandcamp. The band is now focused on developing a live show and has begun writing material for a second album.

items.body: YouTube creator marceve76 has reimagined a-ha‘s 1985 debut album “Hunting High and Low” as if it had been recorded in the 1950s, complete with a mock cover picturing the trio as “The A-Has” in period suits and pompadours. The video, titled “A-Ha – Hunting High And Low, if it was recorded in the 50s,” runs 30 minutes and 20 seconds and covers the album’s full ten-track sequence, including “Take On Me.” The video was already uploaded on November 10, 2025, and has drawn 5,345 views so far. Not a lot that is, despite being one of the better produced videos on his channel, musically speaking. The vocal performance is not Morten Harket’s, and the channel is upfront about the nature of the project, opening with a disclaimer that “voices, faces and characters have no connection to actual people”, and that “the video is an artistic and transformative work made for entertainment purposes.” A recurring format built around AI reinterpretation marceve76 runs a 51,900-subscriber channel built almost entirely around reimagining well-known albums as 1950s recordings, a format that leans on AI music generation, voice and style transfer. Side-Line covered the same creator’s take on Depeche Mode’s “Violator” in July 2025. The “Hunting High and Low” video sits in the same catalog alongside similar treatments of Fleetwood Mac’s “Rumours,” Blondie’s “Parallel Lines,” David Bowie’s “Let’s Dance,” Led Zeppelin’s debut, Dio’s “Holy Diver” and AC/DC’s “The Razors Edge,” among others. The full “Hunting High and Low” tracklist covered in the video, with timestamps: “Take On Me” – 0:00 “Train of Thought” – 2:52 “Hunting High and Low” – 5:52 “The Blue Sky” – 9:09 “Living a Boy’s Adventure Tale” – 12:18 “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.” – 16:12 “And You Tell Me” – 19:44 “Love Is Reason” – 22:20 “I Dream Myself Alive” – 24:52 “Here I Stand and Face the Rain” – 27:17 About a-ha a-ha formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1982, when vocalist Morten Harket joined songwriters Pål Waaktaar and Magne Furuholmen, who had been playing together in earlier Oslo bands. Signed to Warner Bros., the trio released their debut album, “Hunting High and Low,” on June 1, 1985, in Norway and the United States, followed by a UK and European release on October 28 that year. Its lead single “Take On Me” had first been issued in 1984 without success; a 1985 re-release, paired with Steve Barron’s rotoscope-animated video mixing live action and pencil animation, took the song to number one in 36 countries and won six awards at the 1986 MTV Video Music Awards. “Hunting High and Low” also produced the singles “Love Is Reason,” “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.,” “Train of Thought” and the title track. The album has remained a recurring point of reference for the band’s reissue campaigns: Side-Line reported on a 6LP boxset built around the record in January 2023, and on an exclusive 1984 Demos vinyl pressed for Record Store Day 2025. a-ha went on to release albums including “Scoundrel Days” (1986), “Stay on These Roads” (1988), “East of the Sun, West of the Moon” (1990), “Memorial Beach” (1993), and, after a 2000s reunion, “Analogue” (2005), “Foot of the Mountain” (2009), “Cast in Steel” (2015) and “True North” (2022), the latter accompanied by a documentary film. Side-Line covered the 20th-anniversary reissue of “Analogue” as a 2CD deluxe set with a first-time vinyl pressing in February 2026. In June 2025, Morten Harket revealed a Parkinson’s diagnosis, and Magne Furuholmen discussed the band’s creative process in a Side-Line interview earlier that year. “Take On Me” itself continues to draw new versions from other artists, including a 2025 dark cover by Pure Obsessions & Red Nights.

items.body: English post-punk band The Cure may release their fifteenth studio album in November 2026, according to an unconfirmed report. French fan site Pictures of Cure published the claim on July 31, 2026, citing an unnamed source inside Universal, the band’s distributor, who reportedly listed the album in the company’s release schedule for that month. The report was relayed the same day on the fan forum curefans.com, in its “Unconfirmed news and rumours” section. Neither The Cure, frontman Robert Smith, nor Universal has confirmed a release date. Pictures of Cure ties the November claim to two earlier data points: Smith’s remarks during a BBC Radio 6 Music interview recorded on June 6, 2026, in which he said the album was about to be delivered to the label, and the fact that “Songs of a Lost World,” the record Smith has repeatedly described as this album’s companion piece, was released on November 1, 2024. What Robert Smith has said about the album The Cure returned to Rockfield Studios in Wales in March 2025 to record what Smith has described as three albums’ worth of material. Side-Line reported at the time that 13 songs had been recorded. In the June 2026 BBC Radio 6 Music interview, Smith said the second of those three albums is finished and being delivered to Universal. He called it “more dismal than Songs Of A Lost World” and said it is emotionally connected to that album while approaching the material from a different perspective. A third album, drawn from the same sessions, is “really, really upbeat” and “really poppy,” Smith said, with no indication yet of when it might follow. Two songs earmarked for the upcoming album were named by Smith in January 2025: “It Can Never Be the Same,” a song about grief that the band has performed live for years under the earlier title “Christmas Without You,” and “A Boy I Never Knew,” written during the sessions for The Cure’s 2004 self-titled album. Smith has said the album will also include newer, previously unheard material. “Songs of a Lost World” was released on November 1, 2024, through Fiction Records, ending a 16-year gap since “4:13 Dream” (2008). Produced and mixed by Smith with Paul Corkett and recorded at Rockfield Studios, it was the first Cure album written entirely by Smith and gave the band its first UK number one album in 32 years. About The Cure The Cure formed in Crawley, West Sussex, England, in January 1976, when school friends Robert Smith and Michael Dempsey began playing together, initially under the name Malice. The band went through the name Easy Cure before settling on The Cure and signing to Fiction Records, distributed by Polydor, in 1978. The founding lineup of Smith (guitar, vocals), Dempsey (bass) and Lol Tolhurst (drums) released the debut album “Three Imaginary Boys” in 1979. Through numerous lineup changes, with Smith as the only constant member, The Cure built a catalogue running from the austere post-punk of “Seventeen Seconds” (1980) and “Faith” (1981) through “Pornography” (1982), the pop-facing “The Head on the Door” (1985) and “Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me” (1987), to “Disintegration” (1989) and “Wish” (1992), among later releases including “Wild Mood Swings” (1996), “Bloodflowers” (2000), the self-titled “The Cure” (2004) and “4:13 Dream” (2008). The current lineup comprises Robert Smith, Simon Gallup (bass), Roger O’Donnell (keyboards), Jason Cooper (drums) and Reeves Gabrels (guitar). Guitarist and keyboardist Perry Bamonte, who first joined the band in 1984 and rejoined for the “Shows of a Lost World” tour in 2022, died in December 2025 at age 65. The band returned after 16 years away from new albums with “Songs of a Lost World” on November 1, 2024, and confirmed in October 2025 that a follow-up had been recorded at Rockfield Studios. The unconfirmed report of a November 2026 release date would place a new Cure album exactly two years after its predecessor.

items.body: It took the Norwegian duo Kant Kino nearly nine years to release their fourth album. Despite this lengthy hiatus, EBM fans are unlikely to have forgotten the band, as their previous full-length releases were polished, expertly crafted examples of the genre. While EBM remains the album’s primary influence, “Echoes Of The End” also ventures into other sonic territories. The result is a compelling fusion of EBM and Electro-Pop, with occasional touches of Future-Pop. Some tracks recall the melodic approach of Assemblage 23, while the album’s darker moments evoke the early work of Skinny Puppy. At its core, however, “Echoes Of The End” remains a hard-hitting, relentless EBM record, impeccably executed and enriched with vintage-inspired synth textures. The powerful yet controlled vocal delivery perfectly complements the album’s atmosphere. We are treated to no fewer than 24 tracks, although for me the collection is ultimately defined by the irresistible “Choice.” Kant Kino is back—and not a moment too soon. While their sound has evolved, they continue to deliver EBM of the highest caliber. (Rating:8½). Side-Line previously covered the announcement of “Echoes of The End” in April 2026, when the album was confirmed as a digital deluxe edition and a physical 2CD via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Choice”: Choice by Kant Kino About Kant Kino Kant Kino is a Norwegian electronic duo from Oslo, namely Lars Henrik Madsen and Kenneth Fredstie. The project formed after they wrote a tribute track for the ElektroStat festival, after which a Bunkertracks compilation appearance led to their Alfa Matrix signing. The duo’s debut album, “We Are Kant Kino – You Are Not”, appeared in 2010. It was followed by the “LRSBSS EP” on April 15, 2012, then the second full-length “Father Worked In Industry” on February 22, 2013. “Father Worked In Industry” was mixed and mastered by Claus Larsen of Leaether Strip. That release also produced the download singles “Just For The Comfort Of Sleep EP” on March 26, 2013 and “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt EP” on November 22, 2013. While working toward the third album, the band previewed new material with the teaser “Life” in February 2016. While working on a new album, they self-released the Motörhead/Kraftwerk hybrid “We Are The Roadcrew (Robots)” on December 16, 2016, ahead of “Kopfkino”, which was released on Alfa Matrix on January 13, 2017. In May 2017, Alfa Matrix built the first “Matrix:Reb00ted” volume around Kant Kino remixes. The duo later appeared on the Coldkill vs Kant Kino EP “Silent Morning” in 2018, released the Depeche Mode cover single “Pimpf and Touch Faith” in September 2019, and self-released “Enough! (Demo)” on June 30, 2022. Kenneth Fredstie in the meantime mastered “Face The Beat: Session 3” and Kant Kino contributed “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt (Video Edit)” and “Life (No Fucking Guitars Edit)” to the Face The Beat series. They also contributed a remix for Modulo One’s “No Way to Win”, and remixed the Side-Line charity single “Ukraina” in December 2022. In February 2026, Kant Kino returned with “Rodney: End-State Variations”, followed by the fourth album “Echoes Of The End”, reviewed above.

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
Dean Blunt’s totemic, genre-agnostic first ’Black Metal’ album is back in circulation on the heels of its killer 2nd volume, singing out a singular sort of mid-decade London blooz where his myriad circles run into one.

In 2014 ‘Black Metal’ arrived as Blunt’s 4th solo album in a string of quietly groundbreaking and guess-again solo recordings following the break-up of Hype Williams, his duo with Inga Copeland. It was an instant fave, raved about everywhere, and with the benefit of hindsight is arguably one of the past decade’s definitive highlights; a record symptomatic of the way staid generic borders were dissolving, expressing a lucid but woozy pathos that still feels timeless, yet very much of its flat-time, when the stream of musical history had pooled into the reservoir of the internet.

Returning to its slow baked charms years later ‘Black Metal’ has lost none of its allure, with a reflective stillness still belying its depths. Nimbly joining wipe clean presets and crisp licks of original instrumentation with vocals by Blunt and regular spar Joanne Robertson, their baker’s dozen tunes somehow consolidate aspects of everything from hip hop to chamber music, indie-pop to R&B with experimental wit and ohrwurming magick that places it among his most memorable and surprising records.

From the symphonic Americana lilt of ‘Lush’ to its amazing 13 minute centrepiece of chamber soul gauze ‘Forever’ and the free jazz meets folk and roadrap synthscape of ‘Grade’ it coolly piques curiosity and perplexes from every angle, resolving unfamiliar styles with a pop-sharpened manner that follows a path first taken by A.R. Kane and which quite possibly ignited a reappraisal of the problematic way in which Black music has been perceived and categorised in popular/critical culture.

All time business = unmissable.

items.body:
Future modal jazz dub, heard thru a Y2K lens by legendary blowers Pharaoh Sanders & Graham Haynes, and diffused in Bill Laswell’s illbient dub style & pattern. A slept-on, cross-generational ace sure to pique interest FFO Jon Hassell to Talvin Singh, Lászlo Hortobágyi to Material.

Cooked up in NYC’s jazz crucible in 2003 as a duo of Sanders & Haynes - now re-mantled as a Sanders x Laswell session for its first vinyl cut - ‘With a Heartbeat’ speaks to the rich confluence of deeply rooted, forward-thinking jazz with ambient dub that tilted from the late C.20th into this century. Centred on the human heartbeat, it unfurls at a rested systolic throb in two landscaped-scale works which bookend deeper dives into Indian raga and tabla actions, the latter of which may find favour on open-minded ‘floors, due to its effortless, toes-off-the-ground levity. But essentially, it’s idealised for floating at home or road tripping on the astral highway.

Bill Laswell’s name at the top signifies his integral input, but with no discount to Graham Hayne’s cornet, beautifully knit in warm, rising air with his peer, pioneering tenor sax player Pharaoh Sanders, who brings a half century of chops with Coltrane, Sharrock, and myriad others, to the plate. Quite simply it’s a lush listen from front to back, opening from heartical subbass pulse into 17 mins of dusted illbient dub with a cool reserve on ‘Across Time’, and shoring up in almost big beat 4th world fusion scapes reminding of the eL-Hortobãgyi Hortator album with ‘Gamaka’.

Yet we’re most partial to the midsection, where Sanders & Haynes colour the luxuriant space and rolling ballast with a wider range of brass and woodwind in the dewy raga of ‘Morning Tala’, and Trilok Gurtu’s undulating and spicy tabla and scatting vox evoke an aerial game of hashed-out kabaddi in ‘Alankara’.

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

items.body:
2nd wave dub techno staple Stephen Hitchell meets new wave producer Federson in a back ’n forth of timeless originals and versions.

San Francisco’s Chris Kelly, aka Federsen’s Alt Dub label hosts this passing of the baton/torch with CV313 and Echospace figure Hitchell a sits 2nd release after the ‘Positive Charge’ EP  christened the vessel in earlier ’24. Federsen fronts the session with a smoky, night-driving dub of CV313’s ‘Skycrossing’ in properly classic Maurizio style, especially that scooping bassline, whilst shutting it down with the more air-stepping levity of his dusted congas and distant dub chords to ‘Skyway’.

CV313’s original ‘Skycrossing’ places his mastery of constantly shifting, ever the same, dynamic within its unfurling envelopes, alongside a remix of ‘Skyway’ that plunges upward, outward into billowing electro-acoustic dub techno dimensions.

items.body:
On a label full of weirdos, outliers, mavericks and freaks, clandestine Greek anomaly Aeson Zervas is Heat Crimes’ OG wildcard, landing a debut album a couple of years ago that sounded like The Caretaker channeling crates of rebetika, and now returning with this deeply elusive new LP of plasmic synths that unfolds in ways that will leave you with a proper motion sickness of time travel. Aye, it’s a special one.

After lighting up 2024 with blink ’n miss LP & tape drops, Aeson Zervas’s 3rd instalment dips into a perpetual night world of cobwebbed keyboard melodies and flame flicker incantations designed to score your next regression session. As ever, the label and artist remain tight-lipped about pretty much everything, but the vibe is self-evidently clammy and febrile thru a dozen parts familiar to both preceding drops, woven between pillars of inspiration in lemniscate loops and free flowing rhythmelodic arrangements that bind his ideas to bezonked minds.

The Mesolonghi-based enigma continues to prove a master of hypnosis and a conduit for ancient spirits seeping into the modern world, luring susceptible minds to states of bliss and dread, but not without that sense of romance that also lit up his prior releases. Once again feeling the same pull of past worlds as The Caretaker, only slanted to microtonal scales, his mix of lopped-off and extended melodies tell arcane stories still salient to contemporary imaginations able to tune in.

Activating with a section of meditative, almost no-wave strafing discord, themes of shimmering exotica slide into backyard ritualism, with a lilting marimba sounding like it escaped a Martin Denny side before bleeding into a Giallo-esque wheeze, thru port and island-hopping rebetika, and properly haunting passages of midnight sacred music swarmed by cicadas. The 6th (Χωρίς τίτλο 23) part of needling Italianate arps and screeches is particularly affective, as is the plugged-in folkdance sputter of the 8th (Χωρίς τίτλο 25), and a final couplet coming off like Muslimgauze with a thing for sleazy horror, not dub.

Basically, whatever this label serve, lap it up while you can.

items.body:
Lovers of ZudRangMa, Khruangbin, and even the White Lotus 3 soundtrack will be enchanted with Korlakang’s chiming, low-slung meld of ’70s psych pop and Luk Thung from the quieter side of Bangkok...

“Korlakang are four young friends from Thonburi, the quieter, canal-laced western bank of Bangkok, where temple bells and river rhythms shape everyday life. Formed from a bond that stretches back to high school hallways and shared university years, the band came together with a sound rooted in Thai traditional music and the warm haze of psychedelic rock.

Their debut 7-inch, Samong Sai, is that rare thing: a record that seems to arrive already aged, carrying the grain and warmth of a forgotten 70s pressing. It seeps in slowly, sweet and chill, like sound faintly coming through a neighbour's window. The kind of music that makes you stop what you're doing just to hear a little more of.”

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.

items.body:
Nueen follows production for Iceboy Violet and a string of releases for Quiet Time Tapes, Good Morning Tapes and Balmat, with a sprawling new album for 3XL, an ambient drill epic featuring guest spots from Dawuna, Space Afrika, Loraine James, Xzavier Stone and RenzNiro.

Everything clicked into place for Nacho Pezzati when he turned the humid soundscapes of his early releases into distorted beds for Iceboy Violet's casual free associations on the Hyperdub-released ‘You Said You'd Hold My Hand Through the Fire' back in 2024. He retains the same energy on 'Swerved', working alongside a team of vocalists and collaborators to locate a sweetspot between rap, dub and ambient vistas. His methodology is laid bare on 'Searchtiers', obscuring its UK drill-style sliding bass with weightless synths and gaseous FX, upping the ante when vocalist and producer Xzavier Stone jumps on the mic on 'Nowhere Near A Section'. The addition of proper hooks, adlibs and rhymes - "let it burn like Usher Raymond" - makes the production hit that much harder, not just referencing radio rap and R&B but challenging the paradigm. Fittingly, Loraine James, who early on inhabited similar zones, lends her voice to the grimy 'Atmosphere is my Style', whispering over Pezzati's hair metal samples and booming 808 Mafia-style basses. 

Manny's own RenzNiro checks in on 'Impls', rhyming over one of Nueen's most decisive beats, all clipped snares, gong samples and tweaked bass. And Space Afrika turn up with an assist on the low-slung highlight 'Shm', a smoove and sensual D'Angelo-style soul banger with none other than Dawuna on the mic. Dawuna returns on 'Matrix', splitting duties with Xzavier Stone who provides an impressive '00s post-jiggy hook and Pezzati's vision materialises. The haze of half-remembered bites of cloud rap, pop and club rap represents a post-P2P hauntology that's global, not really localised. And connecting with Space Africa again on the closing track 'I Guess', he travels beyond the boundaries of the album itself, lavishing SA's orchestral cries with fuzzy synths and swirling vocals.

items.body:
Mike Paradinas picks 18 scuzzy examples of Nondi_’s wistful take on footwork, ambient noise, and dub techno as an addendum to a strong eponymous 2nd album, nodding to precedents from Actress, AFX, µ-Ziq...

"Following her acclaimed 2023 release Flood City Trax, a dreamy, lo-fi take on footwork inspired by the crumbling rust-belt city she calls home, Nondi returns to Planet Mu with her second self-titled album, Nondi…

While Nondi… retains some of the hazy, nostalgic atmosphere of Flood City Trax, it pushes her sound in bold new directions. “I made this album to capture the sense of freedom I used to get from music when I was first discovering it all,” Nondi says. “It’s meant to be cute, fun, kinda weird and emotional — but most of all, it’s a presentation of some of the prettiest tracks I’ve made.” Though she hasn’t really experienced club culture where she lives, her impressionistic productions evoke the surreal, lingering sounds of a night out — the melodic haze that hums in your ears as you drift off to sleep. Lo-fi and melodic, yet fluid and free, her music carries a sense of flight and intuitive logic. Nondi’s influences range widely — Actress, Aphex Twin, footwork, and the stranger edges of dub techno are all felt, yet she hallucinates them through her own weathered, dreamlike lens. Her tracks often build from clashing loops that evolve and transform organically, or from familiar genre elements reshaped by her instinct for misty, heart-wrenching melody. Nondi… is a uniquely moving and exploratory album that expands her sonic world even further. Lo-fi yet luminous, playful yet profound."

items.body:
Peak Oil mooch in our back yard again with a strong album from YOUTH & Shotta Tapes alum Leo - the latest in their line of UK mutants (Paperclip Minimiser, Low End Activist, Wrecked Lightship) and a definitive statement of classic uk dub-as-method in electroid 2-step and crooked dembow forms.

A whirring cog in the Manchester machine, Leo has spent the 2020s rent in brooding negative space. His 4th album, ‘Cicada Burnt’ emerges in six segments that harness his drummer’s sleight of hand and feel for textured production on structures that teem with hi-tech sound design, insectoid detail and weathered pressure systems. No doubt it’s his most impressive artistic statement thus far, straddling key, extramusical reference points nabbed from his roots in Pennine Oldham landscapes and work strafing the industrial city downhill, and in that sense comparable with the Skam/NMB nexus or DDS’ cloud-seeding rufige.

Under the ochre artwork of Sean Clarke, who does Leo’s live visuals, the album smoulders with a dusky light and particulates in the air, conjuring immersive environmental settings and subtle tensions between the anticipatory rhythms and dread gloom. We can hear coruscating echoes of Paperclip Minimiser’s pendulous metric intricacy via Autechre in ‘Qwershape’, and his adroit percussive instincts on the tight electro-rolls of a ‘Jetti’ reminding us of Gescom's Cybotron-sampling classic 'Puzl', as well as low key Skam legend Mike Williamson - the guy behind that sick Grace Jones edit on Mask 400. His feel for syncopated nuance is zipped tightest in the grimy dembow of ‘Descant’, and likewise a weightless ‘Spirit Level (Prescript)’ demonstrating patiently poised, heightened proprioceptions, held in balance with the tendon-twitching steppas closer ‘Spirit Level’.

items.body:
Good Morning Tapes with a fully sick digital steppas session from DJ and rave shotter Carl Luis of the Merger soundsystem - a big look FFO Blazer Sound System, G Version III, and Raime’s ‘Can You Repeat That Please?’ mixtape.

With a steady hand on the FX, Carl Luis treats the dance to over an hour of militant, tuffest pressure and more spangled gems in a crucial style of ’80s & ‘90s JA x UK sound system weaponry. It’s brimming over with the sort of propulsive, trudging and flying steppas that’s lit dances from Brixton to Chapeltown, Hulme to Berlin for the last 40 years, dancing at the square root of so much music we all love - from early bleep ’n bass to jungle, dub techno, broken beat and dubstep - in a very particular style and pattern. 

Plastic horn pomp ramps with seismic subby tremors and sizzling drum machines in myriad formations, strafing from a late ‘80s zinger, shades away from darkest new beat monk chants, thru 8-bit cone quakers and knees-ups jogged with judicious digits on the dial, to a notable balmier, woozier B-side where his feel for atmospheric levity and hypnotic velocity really comes into play.

items.body:
Belgian jazz wizard Casimir Liberski re-interprets Kōji Kondō's iconic 'The Legend of Zelda' soundtracks on 'The Z Suites', using the recognizable cues as jumping off points for his trio's Ornette Coleman-inspired modern jazz.

How much patience you'll have for this one depends on your interest in Zelda, no doubt. Because from the opening seconds of the 15-minute 'Overworld Suite', it's clear that 'The Z Suites' is Zelda first. The trio of Liberski, bassist Janos Bruneel and drummer Diogo Alexandre clearly love the source material, trekking through all the important moments from 'Ocarina of Time', 'Link's Awakening', 'A Link to the Past' and the original game that started it all. But we have to wonder whether there would ever be a moment to reach for this rather than play Kondō's timeless originals.

items.body:
Inspired by Shigeru Miyamoto's iconic 'The Legend of Zelda' games, cellist and composer Patrick Belaga imagines his latest full-length as a map of fantastical locations, using the language of 20th century minimalism and Coil's unsettling soundscapes to provoke exploration rather than resolution.

When you cite video games as a reference, you can guarantee that almost anyone reading will immediately bring to mind their favorite cues: the low-bitrate Russian folk variations of 'Tetris' or the ubiquitous 'Super Mario Bros' theme. Unexpectedly, these aren't the reference points Belaga makes on 'Solar Calf'. Rather, his interest is in a game's playability, how the meticulously programmed environments allow players to navigate the story in their own way, moving from area to area and sometimes avoiding the core narrative altogether. The concept provided him with a way of swerving the expectation to produce an album that reads beginning to end like a book or a movie and approach it like a game designer instead, considering non-linear listening.

Even the sounds are designed to mimic the aesthetics of a game, not really the clusters of phrases and SFX featured in the background music. As you might expect if you've heard Belaga's previous material, his PAN debut 'Blutt' or his collaboration with Asma Maroof and Tapiwa Svosve 'The Sport of Love', he plays a selection of instruments, but mixes up these sounds with samples, even re-sampling his playing to muddy the picture even more. He's eager to make his landscape as confusing as it is inviting and the compositions themselves, stuttering Reich-ian phrases and Glass-style repetitions that give just a casual glance to Koji Kondo's 'Ocarina of Time' OST, continue the concept, playing like interlocking puzzles that work best shuffled, replayed and engaged with differently each time.

items.body:
Bewitching, sound sensitive and psychedelic experiments from LA’s Celia Hollander ($3.33), landing somewhere between Carl Stone and Laurel Halo...

“Celia Hollander works with digital audio as a medium to intuitively form temporal experiences. Each song in Recent Futures aspires towards a different type of temporal movement: a swing between the recent past and near future, an accelerating present, a temporal eddy, a juxtaposition between massive and microscopic durations, a flowing momentum and a preserved stillness. An assemblage of field recordings drenched, sampled, tumbled, stretched, diced, dyed, layered and reversed, Recent Futures yields varying terrains of the abstracted mundane, a magical realism of audio. 

Celia Hollander is an LA based composer and artist working with audio, scores, performance, installation and text. Her work critically engages ways that audio and the act of listening can shape temporal perception, generate narratives, question cultural infrastructures and cultivate social connection. Her work has been performed or installed in venues and institutions including MOCA, The Getty, Kunsthalle Basel, Cirrus Gallery LA, Human Resources LA and Zebulon, LA and she is a resident dj on Dublab Radio.”

items.body:
Weird America instigator and survivor Sir Richard Bishop expands his hillbilly series with an album of raw, unplugged "moonshine-drunk" sex jams... really.

Last year, Bishop reminded us that the so-called "American Primitive" genre, or at least the legion of John Fahey-inspired guitarists who drew on ragas and American folk music with equal amounts of zeal, were being "way too safe". His prescription was an unrefined, crude style that went back to real basics; gone was the pomp and circumstances of the bourgeois avant-garde and in walked Schrödinger's hillbilly - an avatar he embodied on the pretty self-explanatory 'Hillbilly Ragas'. And he goes a step further into polite societal discomfort on 'Hillbilly Erotica', picking up where its predecessor left off but heading towards the bedroom, boldly asserting that contemporary experimental folk music doesn't need to be sexless.

Fittingly, his titles circle the same territory, approaching erotica not from a sanitised vantage point but from the South with its funk and humidity. The rush of 'Lick Skillet' draws us in and Bishop's already on top form, showing that he doesn't need any embellishment at all to do his thing. And by 'Finger, Tennessee', he's in a genuinely romantic mood, creating a fingerstyle version of what might as well be the outro to a romantic comedy. Thankfully, we're in more familiarly raga-inspired territory on 'Sweet Lips Spiritual' and that's where Bishop really shines, spotlighting the sensuality of a musical form that has its roots in midnight performances by candlelight. If there's a weirder record of late-night gear this year, we'll be surprised.

items.body:
Scott Avery’s Motor City techno label pay homage to Japan’s jazz kissa cafés with a reflective suite of 313 ambient and beatdown advised to admirers of Carl Craig & Detroit Escalator Company...

‘Kissa’ quietly diverges from 48208 World’s usual tuff knocks for a sublime, 8-part album swanning from dreamy, floating vignettes to bittersweet beatdown house nuanced with a mix of Japanese and Detroit late night je ne sais quoi. Tokyo’s clandestine back street jazz listening bars prompt Anthony “Mathias” R. to play it down, in-the-pocket, in procession from the Radiophonic siren of ‘Moonlit Steep’, thru the echoes of Neil Ollivierra’s The Detroit Escalator Company on ‘Kissa’, or C2-esque arp flutters in ‘Velvet Oolong’. He coaxes a certain, tangy tone from his kit on ‘Yuza Drift’ like some imaginary Susumu Yokota meets Howard Thomas joint, and winks at Japanese ambient electronics in ‘Sakura Steam’, saving a real beatdown pearl for those willing to dive deeper in ‘Amber Infusion’.

items.body:
In physical stature and imaginative scope, Luc Ferrari’s 10 x CD / 11 Hour selection for INA GRM’s series presents a poetic building block of C.20th electronic music from the founding director of the GRM in 1958, presenting a unique art history spanning six decades of ingenious, beguiling soundcraft.

Part of a legendary series including titles by concrète pioneers Pierre Schaefer & Pierre Henry, plus weighty surveys of Bernrad Parmegiani, Éliane Radigue and François Bayle, this lavish boxset of Luc Ferrari’s work is a masterclass exploration of avant garde form and function that charts experimental music’s research and development during a radical phase. While even the notion of such a large storage device for sound was unimaginable when Ferrari began making his cut-up musical collages and sound poetry in the ‘50s, his ‘L’Œuvre Électronique’ covers the progression of musical technology and thought from its most laboriously executed origins, working with tape and raw blocks of sound, to the grander digital staging of his ‘90s and early ‘00s radio plays, plotted for multiple voices and spatialised landscapes. 

Collected, this set forms an incredible deep dive into art-music history where the materiality of sound is questioned and reconsidered in relief of its musical connotations, creating in the process a peerless body of work that better approximates the texture of dreams or the audness of waking life than any song, and has long informed the approach to sound organisation by a host of progressive artists, effectively bridging the conceptual precedents of Varèse and Cage and the contemporary futures projected by Lee Gamble or Valerio Tricoli.

The 98 tracks from 31 releases, clocking up just over 10 hours of recordings, delineate across decades following Ferrari’s studies with Messaien and Honegger in the mid ‘50s, and a period of illness that made him better acquainted with the radio receiver, and pioneers such as Schöneberg and Webern, to his co-founding of the Groupe de Recherches Musicales with Schaeffer and François-Bernard Mâche in 1958, and thru his landmark transformation of field recordings made on a Yugoslavian beach, and the ravishing abstractions of later electronic works. 

Until his passing, aged 76 in Arezzo, Italy, Ferrari remained ceaselessly active both in his own practice and teaching, and was revered as the poet of musique concrète. He bought a particularly gallic purview to the paradigm, especially when considered against the more hard-nosed academic pursuits of his peers, making singular use of vocals as an elusive or sometimes literal presence in his works in a way that others didn’t, and as such his works all hare a certain liminal quality that appears richly seductive to fans of fantasy storytelling as much as psychedelic soundtracks and sound as dreamfood imagery.

items.body:
The classic 12 disc Parmegiani Box Set finally given a reissue by INA GRM, covering the majority of Parmegiani's musique concrète output recorded between 1964 and 2007. Is there a more important, influential, totemic single-artist collection in all of electronic music?

The Wire magazine described it as a "bargain price treasure chest....containing worlds of inexhaustible spaciousness and strangeness" and, indeed, listening through just some of the 12 cd's included you find yourself drawn into a multi-faceted world full of timeless treasure.

Parmegiani was mentored by the founding father of Musique Concrète, Pierre Schaeffer, who made use of technological advances that gave the world magnetic tape and microphones to pioneer a method taking everyday noise and transforming them into unrecognisable sounds, a style that became known as Acousmatic music. 

Parmegiani would go on to make use of these Acousmatic techniques in creating a body of work which is not only one of the most significant of the 20th century, but also hugely influential on a whole host of musical pioneers that would follow in his wake, with Christian Fennesz, Aphex Twin, Kode9 and Jim O'Rourke being notable disciples in the contemporary field. 

It’s hard to comprehend let alone articulate the immersive and often woozy effect of these recordings, ranging from eerie cut-out tape loops through to popular music plunderphonics and proto-distilled-dub that's impossible to absorb in one sitting. In short, L’Œuvre Musicale is one of the most impressive and important collections of electronic music you'll likely ever hear, but also one of the most rewarding.

items.body:
Brownswood presents JOY from Isaiah Collier.

"In a world currently defined by unrest, uncertainty, and cultural fracture, acclaimed saxophonist, composer, and bandleader Isaiah Collier returns with Joy, a 5-track EP that reframes one of humanity’s most nuanced emotions both as a devotional grounding and political act. 

Collier’s deeply personal compositions present joy as an act that isn’t rooted in escapism or abstraction, but rather, as something hard-won rooted in lived experience, shaped by transformation, and sustained through connection. Throughout the album’s five compositions, Collier positions joy as a guiding light during challenging times, an expression of challenging yourself to utilize your gifts, an affirmation of love and discovery, and as an affirmative source of reassurance."

“Black Taffy (Donovan Jones) is a Dallas-based composer and performer whose current focus lies in pairing ambient music with big bass and percussion. 

The first born son of Pentecostal music ministers, Donovan grew up witnessing the power music has to induce trance and encourage spiritual awakening. Eventually drawing parallels between christianity, voodoo, and the occult, Jones left the former to immerse himself in the latter. 

Sometimes performing with only Vibraphone and cassette decks, he frequently employs the use of tape loops and other antiquated mediums to create pillowy worlds of wow and flutter.”

items.body:
Codeine, Elliott Smith and Cancer House fiends will be in their element with the bittersweet slowcore and swoon of Goldenstar’s debut, a fine new addition to the Montreal scene, fixed up with engineering/mix/master by Francis Latreille (Priori and Patrick Holland (Project Pablo).

"goldenstar is a band from Montreal. Chamber Music is their EP. It’s out on OST. It takes them to the altar of a relatively new but already widely resonant North American musical canon: it’s a self-avowed slowcore record, a term that conjures intimacy, slow-glowing guitars, and ride cymbals that bathe and shimmer. It’s a term fraught with the legacy of universally beloved forebears like Duster, Bedhead, Codeine, et al. A pantheon of sorts. Slowcore carries weight. But this is no retread. Chamber Music’s palette is recognisable, but reconstituted through the idiosyncrasies of its songwriting: the creeping unease on opener ‘Forget’ and the sleepwalking lamentation of ‘Spinning Out’, songs whose warmth are framed by an ever-present anxiety that ebbs and bobs like lantern light on ocean water.

‘Thread’ unspools a kind of shaky optimism, undercutting every swell of hope with a chord change that eases the realisation of its falseness. The downcast note it ends on is carried through to the EP’s second half, which brings the pace down to a hypnotic sway. ‘Belemen’ and ‘April 3’ are scenic views through tired, dark-circled eyes, twinges of memories felt but elusive, meaning that recedes further every time it’s recalled. Instrumental closer ‘I Blink and See Nothing’ concludes numbly, spiralling downwards like a stomach butterfly turned to a moth. These are songs that speak to stillness and solitude and slow-burning pangs of regret: words unheard and half-thoughts left unspoken, a creeping sense that taking your own advice will only ever reveal the meaning it lacks. It’s about hollowness, it’s music that constructs a chamber in the familiar surroundings of a well-worn void. Welcome down."
